history: The surname Ding has multiple origins. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), there were two dukes with the posthumous name Ding, namely Duke Ding of Qi and Duke Ding of Song. It is said that after their deaths, each of their descendants adopted Ding as their surname. Meanwhile, among Chinese Muslims who descend from Central Asian travellers, Ding is thought to have originated from the Arabic honourific “ud-Din” or “al-Din”.

The surname Wan has two different origins, the first of which can be traced to Rui Bo Wan (芮伯万), ruler of the ancient state of Rui during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). Rui Bo Wan showed too much favouritism to his concubines, which resulted in him being banished to the region of Wei (located in present-day Shanxi province). Some of his descendants adopted his name, Wan, as their surname. The second origin traces its roots to Bi Wan (毕万), a high-ranking official in the state of Jin whose descendants would later establish the powerful state of Wei (魏). Some of his descendants also adopted Wan as their surname.

The surname Qiao can trace its roots to the Yellow Emperor. When the Yellow Emperor died, he was buried in a place called Qiaoshan (桥山), located in present-day Shaanxi province. His descendants who stayed at Qiaoshan to guard his tomb would adopt Qiao (桥) as their surname. During the Northern and Southern Dynasties (420-589), Empeoer Xiaowu of Northern Wei was escaping from the grasp of his regent, Gao Huan, and sought refuge under the general Yuwen Tai. One of Emperor Xiaowu’s officials, Qiao Qin (桥勤), also followed him. It was then that Yuwen Tai made Qiao Qin change his surname from Qiao (桥), meaning “bridge”, to Qiao (乔), meaning “tall”. Hence, the surname Qiao as we know it today was born.

From the name of the ancient state of Yu (邘), located in present-day Henan province. After King Wu of Zhou overthrew the Shang Dynasty, he granted the state of Yu to his second son Yu Shu (邘叔). This state was later conquered by the state of Jin (晋), and Yu Shu’s descendants took on the surname Yu (于), dropping the part of their original name meaning “country” (阝).

The surname Ren can trace its roots to the Yellow Emperor. It is said that the Yellow Emperor had 25 sons, one of whom was Yuyang (禺阳). Yuyang was granted the region of Ren in present-day Shandong province, and his descendants would later adopt Ren as their surname.

This distinct Wu surname originated in the State of Chu, in present-day Hubei and Hunan provinces. According to legend, Wu Xu served as an official during the reign of the Yellow Emperor and descended from the Mi imperial family line, with his descendants adopting the Wu surname. An alternative origin traces the name to the Zhou dynasty's household management system, in which officials overseeing units of five households were addressed as "wu bo," a title that eventually became a hereditary family surname.

This surname can be traced back to the royal family of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC). Cheng Wang, the second king of the Zhou dynasty, was granted the state of Han 韩, in present-day Shaanxi province. When the state of Han was later annexed by the state of Jin, members of the royal family scattered. Those that settled further south in the area of the Yangtze and Huai rivers found that the character for their old kingdom, "Han" was pronounced "He" in this area, and so changed their name to a character more widely pronounced He.

The Yu surname traces back to ancient China through two primary accounts. One credits Youyu, an official under Duke Mu of Qin during the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC), who helped establish Qin as a regional power and pioneered concepts of benevolent governance. An alternative account links the surname to descendants of Yu the Great, the legendary ancient emperor, specifically through his youngest son Sihan, who was appointed King of the Yu territory.

The surname Hou can trace its origins to Marquis Min of Jin (晋侯缗), who lived during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). Marquis Min was overthrown by his relative, who would become the new Duke Wu of Jin. Marquis Min’s descendants escaped from the state of Jin, and adopted Hou (侯) as their surname, which means “marquis” in Chinese.

The surname Fu has two different origins, the first of which can be traced back to a man named Fu Yue (傅说). It is said that during the Shang Dynasty, King Wu Ding (武丁) was looking for a capable minister who could help him restore the country’s former glory, when he dreamt of a man named Yue. Convinced that Yue was the minister he sought after, the king ordered his men to look for Yue. Yue was eventually found at a place called Fuyan (傅岩) in modern Shanxi province, a slave who built rammed earth walls. Upon talking to Yue, King Wu Ding was impressed by his abilities and made Yue prime minister, after which the country prospered once more. Yue was bestowed with the surname Fu, which his descendants still bear till this day. The second origin involves Dayou (大由), a descendant of the Yellow Emperor who was granted the land of Fu (傅). His descendants also came to adopt Fu as their surname.

There are two main sources for the Guan surname. According to one account, the Guans are descended of a Grand Minister called Guan Fenglong, who lived during the Xia Dynasty. The family settled in modern-day Shanxi Province, and later prospered in Gansu Province.

According to another account, the surname is derived of an official post called the "Guanling" or the "Director of the Pass". Guanling was the official guard at strategic points along the borders, responsible for protecting the realm against foreign intruders. The surname Guan was later adopted by any descendants of those who held this post. These descendants primarily settled in Shandong and Jiangsu provinces. 

The surname is popular today among ethnic minorities such as the Zhuang people and the Mongols.

From the name of the city of Feng, in the state of Wei during the Zhou dynasty (1046 - 256 BC). The fifteenth son of the virtuous duke Wen Wang, Bi Gonggao, was granted the state of Wei soon after the founding of the Zhou dynasty. A later descendant named Bi Wan was granted Feng city, and his descendants took the city name as their surname.

The Liu surname has several legendary origins, the most prominent tracing back to Liu Lei, a legendary "Keeper of Dragons" during the Xia dynasty. The surname rose to widespread prominence through Liu Bang, who rose from peasant origins to found the Han dynasty around 206 BC. Reigning as Emperor Gaozu, he popularised the surname Liu further by conferring it on favoured subjects as a mark of imperial favour. As of 2019, Liu ranked as China's fourth most common surname, claimed by roughly 70 million people.

The surname Lu can trace its roots back to Gao Xi (高傒), a Qi nobleman in the 7th-century BC. In 686 BC, Duke Xiang of Qi was murdered by his cousin Wuzhi (无知), who then usurped the Qi throne. With Gao Xi’s help, Wuzhi was killed and Duke Xiang’s younger brother, Prince Xiaobai (小白) came to power. Prince Xiaobai would come to be known as Duke Huan of Qi, one of the most powerful rulers during the Spring and Autumn period (771 - 476 BC). As a reward, Gao Xi was granted the region of Lu in present-day Shandong province, and his descendants later adopted Lu as their surname.

The surname Shi can trace its roots back to Yin Yi (尹佚), a court historian at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC). He was well-respected for his sense of righteousness and responsibility as a historian. Some of Yin Yi’s descendants would eventually come to adopt Shi (史) as their surname, in honour of their ancestor’s role as a court historian, or taishi (太史) in Chinese.

The Ye surname traces its origins to the city of Ye in the State of Chu during the Spring and Autumn period. The lineage descends from Yuxiong, a descendant of the Yellow Emperor, whose great-grandson Xiong Yi received the fiefdom of Chu. Following the Battle of Boju, Shen Zhuliang was enfeoffed with the frontier city of Ye and became known as the "Duke of Ye" (叶公), serving as a general and prime minister. The Ye name became synonymous with power, prestige, and a lineage traced back to the Yellow Emperor himself.

From the name of the ancient state of Lü, in present-day Henan province. Boyi (伯夷), a descendant of the Yan Emperor, had assisted Yu the Great in controlling the legendary great floods that plagued China for at least two generations. In recognition of Boyi’s contributions, Yu the Great granted him the state of Lü. During the Spring and Autumn period (771 - 476 BC), the State of Lü was conquered by the State of Chu, after which Boyi’s descendants adopted Lü as their surname.

The Wu surname originated from the ancient state of Wu in present-day Jiangsu province. During the 13th century BC, two sons of King Tai of Zhou, Taibo and Zhongyang, relocated southeast and established this powerful state, and their descendants subsequently adopted Wu as their surname. One of the most celebrated rulers of Wu was King Helu, regarded as one of the "Five Hegemons of China" during the Spring and Autumn period, cementing the clan's historical prominence.

One of the oldest Chinese surnames, Zhou is also the name of the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC), when many current Chinese surnames first came into use. According to legend, Jiang Yuan, a concubine of the legendary emperor Ku in the 25th century BC, accidentally stepped in the imprint of a god’s big toe, which impregnated her. Not wanting such a child, she abandoned the newborn baby, Hou Ji, in the wilderness. The infant was protected from the elements by the wings of eagles and suckled on the milk of cows and sheep. He learned how to grow grain, and became the minister of agriculture under the legendary emperor Yao. His clan eventually settled in a city named Zhouyuan, in present-day Shaanxi province in western China. Under the influence of the name of the city, they came to be known as the Zhou, even though their surname was originally Ji. This lasted for over a millennium until a descendant, the famed virtuous Duke Wu Wang, changed his surname to Zhou, and his son established the Zhou dynasty.

From a place called Tang, in present-day Shanxi province. The legendary Yellow Emperor (2697–2595 BC) granted this region to his son Dan Zhu, whose descendants eventually adopted it as their surname. They held power in the region until they were conquered by Cheng Wang, second king (1115–1079 BC) of the Zhou dynasty. Cheng Wang granted the region to his brother Shu Yu, whose descendants also adopted the place name Tang as a surname. This character was later used for the Tang dynasty, which lasted between 618 and 907 AD.

The surname Xia can trace its roots to the Yu the Great, an ancient Chinese king who founded the Xia dynasty, traditionally considered the first dynasty in Chinese history. It is said that Yu the Great was famed for subduing the legendary floods plaguing China, through his diligence and engineering work. Emperor Shun, who was the reigning emperor then, was so impressed by Yu’s abilities that he passed the throne to Yu instead of his own son, thus beginning the Xia dynasty. After the Xia dynasty was conquered by the Shang dynasty, following the defeat of its tyrannical last king Jie, some of the Xia dynasty’s descendants adopted Xia as their surname.

The surname Yao is one of the oldest-known surnames in China. The left-half of the word Yao is the word “女”, or “woman”, suggesting that the surname may have existed when China was still a matrilineal society. Legend says that Emperor Shun was born in a place called Yaoxu (姚墟) in present-day Henan province, and adopted Yao as his surname. Many of Emperor Shun’s descendants would later adopt their own surnames, but some retained Yao as their surname till this day.

The surname Jiang is one of the oldest-known surnames in China. The bottom-half of the word Jiang is the word “女”, or “woman”, suggesting that the surname may have existed when China was still a matrilineal society. Legend says that the Yan Emperor was born at the Jiang River (姜水), and would adopt Jiang as his surname. Although many of Yan Emperor’s descendants would later adopt other surnames, some of them retained Jiang as their surname, which has survived till this day.

The surname Kong has multiple origin stories. One of them states that some descendants of King Tang of Shang combined the characters Zi (子), surname of the Shang nobility, and Yi (乙), name of King Tang, to form the word Kong (孔) and adopt it as their surname. Another story traces its roots to Kong Fu Jia (孔父嘉), a nobleman from the state of Song during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). When Kong Fu Jia was killed, his descendants escaped to the state of Lu, and adopted Kong as their surname. One of them was none other than Confucius, one of the most important and influential philosophers in Chinese history, whose teachings still shape East Asian society today.

The Sun clan can trace its origins to King Wen of Zhou, the magnanimous ruler credited with the establishment of the Zhou Dynasty. One of his descendants was Hui Sun, a high official of the state of Wei. In his memory, his descendants adopted Sun as their surname.

The surname Meng has multiple origins. In ancient times, the eldest son born from a concubine would be named Meng (孟), as opposed to the eldest son born from the principal wife who would be named Bo (伯). During the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), Qing Fu (庆父), who was the eldest son born from Duke Huan of Lu’s concubine, attempted to usurp the Lu throne, killing two of his nephews in the process. When Qing Fu died, his descendants adopted Mengsun (孟孙) as their surname, which would later be simplified as Meng. The Confucian philosopher Mencius is said to have descended from this line. Meanwhile, another origin story states that descendants of Duke Ling of Wei’s older brother, Meng Zhi (孟絷), also adopted Meng as their surname.

From a place name, the state of Song. After the Zhou overthrew the corrupt king of the Shang dynasty, Zhou Xin, in 1122 BC, the new Zhou dynasty granted the state of Song to the overthrown king’s half-brother, Wei Ziqi. His descendants eventually adopted Song as their surname. 

This character was later used for the name of the Song dynasty, which lasted between 960 and 1279 AD.

The surname Yin has multiple origins, one of which can trace its roots back to Shaohao (少昊), said to be the Yellow Emperor’s son. Shaohao’s son was granted the city of Yin, located in present-day Shanxi province. His descendants eventually adopted Yin as their surname. Another origin derives from the name of the ancient state of Yin, located in present-day Henan province. The state of Yin was founded by Yin Yi (尹佚), a court historian at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC). Eventually, some of his descendants adopted Yin as their surname as well.

The surname Cui can trace its roots back to Ji Zi (季子), a nobleman from the state of Qi. When Duke Ding of Qi died in 975 BC, Ji Zi, as his eldest son, should have inherited the Qi throne. Instead, he gave up his claim and let his younger brother become the new duke, Duke Yi of Qi. Ji Zi had a fief at the region of Cui, located in present-day Shandong province, and his descendants later came to adopt Cui as their surname.

The surname Chang has multiple origins. During the reign of the Yellow Emperor, there was Chang Yi (常仪) who was in charge of lunar divination, and Chang Xian (常先) who was an official in charge of public works. Their descendants are said to have adopted Chang as their surname. Interestingly, Chang Yi is believed to have inspired the story of Chang’e, the Chinese goddess of the Moon. Another origin story traces the surname Chang back to Wei Kang Shu (卫康叔), younger brother of King Wu of Zhou. A descendant of Wei Kang Shu was granted the region of Chang (常), and thus his descendants adopted Chang as their surname as well.

The surname Kang can trace its roots back to Wei Kang Shu (卫康叔), a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou. Wei Kang Shu was originally granted the region of Kang (located in present-day Henan province), but would later be granted the state of Wei (卫国). Some of Wei Kang Shu’s descendants eventually came to adopt Kang as their surname.

According to legend, the Liaos are descended of the ancient kings of the Zhou dynasty. 

King Wu is credited with overthrowing the Shang Dynasty and establishing the Zhou Dynasty(1046 - 256 BC). He had many brothers, including one named Ji Liao, whom he employed as a high-ranking official. The king granted him the title of "Bo" or "Earl", so Ji Liao came to be known as Liao Bo or Earl Liao. After the king's death, his son Cheng succeeded him. Liao Bo continued to serve in the Zhou Court and helped the new King to govern the fledgling Zhou empire. Liao Bo's offspring adopted Liao as their surname in remembrance of him.

According to legend, the Zhang surname originated with Zhang Hui, grandson of the Yellow Emperor, who was honoured for his expertise in weapon production, particularly bows and arrows - the character 张 itself combines the characters for "bow" and "long." His descendants settled in Qingyang, in modern-day Qinghe county, Hubei, establishing the clan's ancestral homeland. Zhang is the 18th most common surname in China and has spread worldwide through successive waves of migration.

The surname Peng can trace its roots back to Peng Zu (彭祖). A descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu, Peng Zu was skilled at making wild chicken soup, which earned him the recognition of Emperor Yao. As such, Emperor Yao granted the state of Peng (彭) in present-day Jiangsu province to Peng Zu. Interestingly, legend says that Peng Zu lived up to a ripe old age of 800, and was deified upon his passing. His descendants eventually came to adopt Peng as their surname.

The Xu surname traces back to Boyi, a legendary tribal leader of the 2nd millennium BC credited with helping to control the Great Flood. After the state of Xu was conquered by the state of Wu in 512 BC, its descendants adopted Xu as their family name in commemoration of their fallen nation. An alternative origin links the surname to the Rebellion of the Three Guards (1042-1039 BC), when the Duke of Zhou divided Shang dynasty loyalist factions into six clans, one of which bore the Xu name.

The surname Dai has two origins. The first originates from the ancient state of Dai located in present-day Henan province, said to be descended from Shang nobility. After the state of Dai was conquered by the state of Zheng during the Spring and Autumn period (771 - 476 BC), its descendants adopted Dai as their surname. The second origin story states that the surname originates from the posthumous name of Duke Dai of Song, whose descendants later adopted Dai as their surname as well.

The surname Wen has multiple origins. One origin traces its roots to King Wen of Zhou, who was posthumously honoured as the founder of the Zhou dynasty (1046-256 BC). Some of his descendants were said to have adopted Wen as their surname. Another origin story states that the surname Wen came from the founder of the ancient state of Xu, Xu Wen Shu (许文叔). Some of his descendants also came to adopt Wen as their surname.

The surname Fang has two origins. The first originates from Lei (雷), a descendant of the Yan Emperor. Lei fought alongside the Yellow Emperor against Chiyou (蚩尤), and as such was rewarded with the region of Fangshan (方山) in present-day Henan province. Some of his descendants would adopt Fang as their surname. The second origin can trace its roots to Fang Shu (方叔), who was an official during the reign of King Xuan of Zhou (828 BC - 782 BC). Fang Shu was rewarded with the region of Luo (洛) after fighting a victorious battle against the state of Chu, and his descendants would adopt his name, Fang, as their surname.

The surname Yi has two different origins. The first origin traces its roots to the ancient state of Zhongshan, located in present-day Hebei province. When it was eventually conquered by the much more powerful state of Zhao in 296 BC, King Shang of Zhongshan and his people were relocated to present-day Shanxi province, and adopted Yi as their surname. The second origin traces its roots to Jiang Ziya (姜子牙), a military advisor at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC) who would later found the powerful state of Qi. One of his descendants was granted the land of Yi, located in present-day Hebei province. This branch would eventually adopt Yi as their surname as well.

There are two main branches of the Cao surname. The first branch shares a common history with the surname Zhu 朱: at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), Cao Jia, a descendant of the legendary emperor Zhuanxu, was bestowed lordship of the state of Zhu. Later, this state was conquered by the state of Chu. As a result, some of Cao Jia's descendants dropped the part of the surname meaning "country" (阝), indicating that they had been separated from their ancestral home. Another group of his descendants adopted Cao as their surname, in his memory. The Caos thereafter primarily settled in modern-day Shandong province. 

According to another account, the Caos are believed to be descended of the ancient Zhou kings. The surname is derived of a kingdom called the State of Cao, which was bestowed upon Chen Dou by his father, the King Wen of Zhou.

From an ancient state called Céng 鄫, located in present-day Lanling County in Shandong province. The Zengs are descended of the ancient kings of the Xia Dynasty (ca. 2,000 BC). 

The state of Ceng was granted to Qu Lie, son of the emperor Shao Kang. His descendants thereupon adopted the state's name as their surname. In 567 BC, Ceng was annexed by the kingdom of Ju (located in present-day Shandong province), and the crown prince of Ceng fled to Lu Kingdom. From then on, he changed his surname from Ceng 鄫 to Zeng 曾, dropping the part of the surname meaning "country" (阝), so that his descendants would remember they were separated from their ancestral home.

From the name of the ancient state of Zhu 邾, located in present-day Shandong province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), Cao Jia, a descendant of the legendary emperor Zhuanxu, was bestowed lordship of the state of Zhu. Later, this state was conquered by the state of Chu. Cao Jia's descendants fled their state, and from that moment on, dropped the part of the surname meaning "country" (阝), indicating that they had been separated from their ancestral home.

The surname Li evolved from the ancient Ying lineage, descending from Emperor Zhuanxu. Tradition holds that General Gaoyao's descendants first adopted the character 理 (meaning "reason") as their surname. This later changed to 李 ("plum") through a legendary tale: Li Zheng, a minister who opposed the cruel Shang King Zhou, was executed, and his son Li Lizhen survived in hiding by eating wild plums, afterwards changing the family name to Li in gratitude. Li is today one of the most common surnames in China.

The surname Du can ultimately trace its roots back to Emperor Yao. Emperor Yao’s descendant, Liu Lei (刘累), was the Keeper of Dragons for King Kong Jia during the Xia Dynasty. Some of Liu Lei’s descendants, in turn, would be granted the region of Du in present-day Shaanxi province by King Cheng of Zhou. They would later adopt Du as their surname.

The Yang surname originated in Hongnong County, in present-day Henan and Shaanxi provinces. During the Jin dynasty (678-677 BC), Duke Wu conquered the vassal state of Yang and appointed Shu Xiang to govern it. When Shu Xiang's descendants later faced persecution, his great-grandson Yang Dao fled to Hongnong and established the lineage there. An alternative account traces origins to Song dynasty Zhejiang, where a foster child changed his surname to Yang in honour of his caretaker.

The Lin surname originated during the Shang dynasty when Prince Bi Gan's pregnant wife fled into a forest to escape King Zhou's wrath. After the prince's execution and the subsequent fall of the Shang dynasty, the new ruler honoured Bi Gan's loyalty by conferring the surname Lin upon his newborn son, born in hiding. The character 林 combines two "wood" radicals (木木), symbolising a forest. Lin ranks as the 18th most common surname in China and has spread widely through migration to Southeast Asia and beyond.

From the name of Liang Mountain in present-day Shaanxi province. During the reign of Zhou dynasty emperor Xuan Wang (827–782 BC), Qin Zhong set out on an expedition to subdue the barbarians to the west, in Central Asia. Qin Zhong was killed, and his five sons set out to avenge their father, eventually succeeding and defeating the peoples of the west. The emperor divided the area of Shang among them, and the second son received the area around Liang Mountain. His descendants thereafter adopted the surname Liang. In later times, Liang was the name of two Chinese dynasties, the Southern Liang Dynasty (502–557) and the Western Liang Dynasty (907–923).

The surname Wu has multiple origins. One origin story traces its roots back to King Ping of Zhou. When King Ping’s youngest son was born, it was said that the lines on his palm resembled the ancient character for the word Wu, and so this son’s descendants adopted Wu as their surname. Other origins suggest the surname came from King Wu Ding during the Shang Dynasty, or Duke Wu of Song during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC).

The surname Duan can trace its roots to Gong Shu Duan (共叔段), the younger brother of Duke Zhuang of Zheng during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). Gong Shu Duan attempted to usurp the throne from Duke Zhuang but failed, and escaped to the region of Gong (located in present-day Henan province). When Duke Zhuang’s son Duke Li inherited the throne, he invited Gong Shu Duan’s descendants back to the sate of Zheng. These descendants would eventually adopt Duan as their surname.

From the name of the ancient state of Mao, located in present-day Henan province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), Mao Shu Zheng (毛叔郑), younger brother of King Wu of Zhou, was granted the state of Mao. When the state of Mao was eventually conquered by the state of Qin during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), its descendants adopted Mao as their surname.

From the name of the ancient state of Jiang, located in present-day Henan province. Boyi (伯益), a descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu, was granted the state of Jiang at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC). However, being surrounded by powerful states like Chu, Song, and Qi, as well as constant floods from the Huai River, the state of Jiang did not last long. Eventually, it was conquered by the state of Chu, and its descendants adopted Jiang as their surname.

The surname Tang can trace its roots back to King Tang of Shang, the first king of the Shang Dynasty.  Under King Tang’s leadership, the Shang dynasty managed to overthrow the tyrannical King Jie of the previous Xia Dynasty. Eventually, some of King Tang’s descendants would adopt Tang, the posthumous name of their ancestor, as their surname.

The surname Wang is said to have two different origins. The first originates from the ancient state of Wangmang (汪芒), located in present-day Zhejiang province. When the state of Wangmang was conquered by the state of Chu, its descendants settled in present-day Anhui province and adopted Wang, a shortened version of Wangmang, as their surname. The second origin story says that Duke Cheng of Lu granted the region of Yingchuan (颍川) to his second son Wang (汪), and his descendants would come to adopt Wang as their surname.

From the name of the ancient state of Shen, located in present-day Henan and Anhui provinces. During his reign (1042 - 1021 BC), King Cheng of Zhou granted the state of Shen (沈) to his uncle, Ji Zai (季载). The state of Shen was later conquered by the state of Cai during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), after which Ji Zai’s descendants adopted Shen as their surname.

The surname Pan can trace its roots back to Ji Sun (季孙), a grandson of King Wen of Zhou. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), King Wen granted his 15th son, Bi Gong Gao (毕公高), the state of Bi in present-day Shaanxi province. In turn, Bi Gong Gao granted the region of Pan to his son, Ji Sun. Ji Sun’s descendants who later adopt Pan as their surname.

The surname Xiong can trace its roots back to Yu Xiong (鬻熊), an official during the reign of King Wen of Zhou (1125-1051 BC). Yu Xiong was a descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu, and said to have been a teacher of King Wen himself. Yu Xiong’s great-grandson, Xiong Yi (熊绎), would later found the powerful state of Chu. When the state of Chu was eventually conquered by the state of Qin during the end of the Warring States period (475-221 BC), some of its descendants adopted Xiong as their surname, in honour of their ancestor Yu Xiong.

The Wang surname originated when royal descendants of fallen kings adopted the title "wang" (king) as a family name. One account traces it to Bigan, who fell out of favour during the Shang dynasty, with his descendants taking the name Wang in recognition of his royal heritage. Another traces it to Wang Zijin, an exiled son of a Zhou emperor, whose descendants likewise adopted the surname. Wang is today the most common surname in China, comprising over 7.1% of the population, concentrated especially in the northern provinces such as Shandong.

The surname Tian can trace its roots to Chen Wan (陈完), also known as Tian Wan (田完). Chen Wan was originally a prince from the state of Chen, who later escaped to the state of Qi to avoid conflict. Duke Huan of Qi, who reigned from 685 to 643 BC, recognised Chen Wan’s abilities and made him an official. As the ancient pronunciations of Chen (陈) and Tian (田) were similar, Chen Wan was also known as Tian Wan, and his descendants would come to adopt Tian as their surname.

The surname Bai has multiple origin stories. One of them traces its roots back to Bai Fu (白阜), an official during the Yan Emperor’s time who was known for his efforts in dredging waterways. His descendants are said to have adopted Bai as their surname. Another story states that during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), a nobleman from the state of Chu named Bai Gong Sheng (白公胜) attempted to seize the throne from his cousin, Duke Hui of Chu. When he failed, Bai Gong Sheng committed suicide. As he had earlier been granted the region of Baidi (白地), located in present-day Henan province, his descendants adopted Bai as their surname. Notably, Bai is also a major surname among Chinese Muslims, most of whom descend from ancient Central Asian travellers.

The surname Sheng can trace its origins to Shao Gong Shi (召公奭), a high-ranking minister at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046-256 BC). He was granted the state of Yan as a reward for helping King Wu of Zhou overthrow the Shang Dynasty. Some of his descendants adopted his name, Shi (奭), as their surname. During the Han Dynasty, in order to avoid the naming taboo of Emperor Yuan of Han (75-33 BC), whose personal name was Liu Shi (刘奭), Shao Gong Shi’s descendants changed their surname from Shi to Sheng.

The surname Shi can traces its roots to Shi Que (石碏), a senior official from the state of Wei (卫国) during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). In 719 BC, Duke Huan of Wei was murdered by his brother Zhou Yu (州吁), who promptly usurped the throne. In the process, Zhou Yu was assisted by Shi Que’s son, Shi Hou (石厚). Shi Que would later kill Zhou Yu, and install Duke Huan’s other brother Duke Xuan to power. Shi Que also did not hesitate in executing his own son Shi Hou for the latter’s involvement in Duke Huan’s murder, and was lauded for upholding justice at the cost of his blood relation. Shi Que’s descendants would come to adopt Shi as their surname.

The surname Qin has two origins. The first is from the name of the ancient state of Qin, located in present-day Gansu province, which would eventually unify the whole of China under the rule of Emperor Qin Shi Huang. Feizi (非子), founder of the state of Qin, was a descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu, and said to be an expert horsekeeper. Impressed with his capabilities, King Xiao of Zhou granted the region of Qin to him. Some of his descendants would eventually adopt Qin as their surname. The second origin states that one branch from King Wen of Zhou’s descendants was granted another region named Qin, located in present-day Henan province. These descendants would also adopt Qin as their surname.

From the name of the ancient state of Cheng, located in present-day Henan province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), Bofu (伯符) was granted the state of Cheng, in reward for fighting alongside the Zhou kings. Bofu could trace his roots back to Emperor Zhuanxu, who was in turn the Yellow Emperor’s grandson. When the state of Cheng fell during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), its descendants adopted Cheng as their surname.

From the name of the ancient state of Zhang (鄣), located in present-day Shandong province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046-256 BC), the state of Zhang became a vassal state under the state of Qi, ruled by Jiang Ziya (姜子牙). Jiang Ziya then granted the state of Zhang to one of his sons. Eventually, the state of Zhang was conquered by the state of Qi, and its descendants took on the surname Zhang (章), dropping the part meaning “country” (阝).

From the name of the state of Luo, in existence during the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). The state of Luo was granted to a mythical figure called Zhurong, who in folk religion is considered the god of fire and of the south. He is also believed to be descended of the Yellow Emperor. Subsequently, his descendants adopted the state name as their surname.

According to another legend, the Luos are the descendants of an ancient tribe who were responsible for knitting nets for the capture of birds: the character "luo" means "capturing with net".

Shares a common ancestry with the surname Chen 陈. The Hu clan is believed to be descended of the legendary Emperor Shun. When Gui Man was bestowed the state of Chen by the King Wu of Zhou, some of his descendants adopted the surname "Chen" in honor of the newfound state. After his death, Gui Man was granted the posthumous name "Hu Gong", and another group of his descendants adopted "Hu" as their surname, in his honor.

From the name of the ancient state of Su (苏), in present-day Henan province. During the Xia Dynasty, King Huai of Xia granted the region of Yousu (有苏) to Emperor Zhuanxu’s descendant Kunwu (昆吾), which eventually became the state of Su. When the state of Su fell during the Shang Dynasty, its descendants adopted Su as their surname. One of them, Su Fensheng (苏忿生), would later become Minister of Justice (司寇) to King Wu of Zhou, and be granted the state of Wen (温).

The surname Fan can trace its roots back to Emperor Yao. One of his descendants, Shi Hui (士会), was a military commander under the state of Jin, during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). In recognition of his achievements, Shi Hui was granted the region of Fan in present-day Henan province, and would be known posthumously as Fan Wuzi (范武子). His descendants would adopt Fan as their surname as well.

From the name of the ancient state of Xiao (located in present-day Anhui province), a vassal state of the state of Song. The state of Xiao was granted to a Song nobleman named Xiao Shu Daxin (萧叔大心), who had helped Duke Huan of Song regain power over the state of Song from the rebellious Nangong Changwan (南宫长万). After the state of Xiao was conquered by the state of Chu in 597 BC, Xiao Shu Daxin’s descendants adopted Xiao as their surname.

The surname Dong can trace its roots back to the legendary Emperor Zhuanxu. It is said that Dong Fu (董父), a descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu, was skilled in the taming of dragons. Emperor Shun, the emperor at the time, appointed Dong Fu with the job of raising and training dragons. Dong Fu managed to teach the dragons various dances, greatly pleasing Emperor Shun who then granted Dong Fu the land of Zongchuan (鬷川) in present-day Shanxi province, as well as the surname Dong. Today, his descendants still bear the surname of Dong.

From the name of the state of Jiang, in present-day Henan province. The Duke of Zhou was the younger brother and chief adviser of Wu Wang, who established the Zhou dynasty in 1122 BC; his third son, Bo Ling, was granted lordship of the state of Jiang. Bo Ling’s descendants eventually adopted Jiang as their surname.

The Cais are said to be the descendants of the 5th son of King Wen of Zhou, Ji Du. Ji Du was awarded the title of marquis of the State of Cai (in modern-day Henan province), and he was known as Cai Shu Du ("Uncle Du of Cai"). Together with Guan Shu and Huo Shu, they were known as the Three Guards. 

When King Wu died, his son King Cheng was too young to ascend the throne, so his uncle, the Duke of Zhou, became regent. The Three Guards grew jealous of the Duke's power, and joined forces to overthrow him. The Duke of Zhou suppressed their rebellion, and Cai Shu was exiled. Eventually, Cai Shu’s son was named the new Duke of Cai. Some 600 years later in the Warring States period, the State of Chu conquered Cai in 447 BC and was itself conquered by the Qin state which, in turn, formed the Qin Empire, China's first empire. With the spread of family names to all social classes in the new empire, many people of the former state of Cai began to bear it as a surname.

Over the years, the Cais have undertaken two major migrations. During the Huang Chao Rebellion (AD 875) at the end of the Tang Dynasty (AD 618-907), the Cai clan migrated to Guangdong and Fujian provinces. Another later migration occurred when Ming Dynasty loyalist Koxinga moved military officials surnamed Cai and their families to Taiwan in the 17th century. As a result, the surname is far more common in these areas and in areas settled by their descendants (e.g., Southeast Asia) than in other parts of China.

From the name of the ancient state of Xue, located in present-day Shandong province. Xi Zhong (奚仲), a descendant of the Yellow Emperor, was said to have invented the ancient Chinese chariot during the reign of Yu the Great. In recognition of his work, Yu the Great granted Xi Zhong the state of Xue. Xi Zhong’s descendants would later adopt Xue as their surname.

The surname Yuan can trace its roots back to Yuan Taotu (辕涛图), a 7th-century BC nobleman from the state of Chen. Yuan Taotu was granted the land of Yangxia (阳夏) in present-day Henan province, and took the second character in his grandfather’s style name, Boyuan (伯爰), as his own family name. Initially, the surname was written in numerous ways, including “袁”, “辕”, and “爰” (all pronounced Yuan), until the Qin Dynasty (221 - 206 BC) when “袁” emerged as the standardised form still in use today.

According to one legend, this surname can be traced back to the hermit-sage Xu You, who was offered the throne by the mythical Emperor Yao. Upon hearing his proposal, Xu You washed his ears in a river to rid them of such defilement!

Most Xus trace their origin to some 1,000 years later when the first king of the Zhou dynasty granted the area of Xu in present-day Henan province to Wen Shu. Wen Shu's descendants eventually adopted the name of the area of Xu as their surname.

In later times, the Ming and Qing Dynasties saw an unprecedented increase in the Xu population, partly due to the fact that it was adopted by many ethnic minorities.                "

From an area called Xie, in present-day Nanyang of Henan province. Xuan Wang, the penultimate king (827–781 BC) of the Western Zhou dynasty, granted this area to one of his brothers-in-law. The people of Xie later adopted the name of the state as their surname.

In the Eastern Jin dynasty (317 - 120 AD), the Xie were among the cluster of noble clans who fled to the south in the wake of the fall of the capital of Chang'an, dominating the court thereafter.

From the ancient state of Tan in present-day Shandong province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC), a descendant of Yu the Great was granted the state of Tan. However, it would later be conquered by Duke Huan of Qi in 683 BC. The descendants of the state of Tan later adopted Tan as their surname.

The surname He can trace its roots to Duke Huan of Qi. One of his great-grandsons, Qing Feng (庆封), adopted Qing as his surname, in honour of his father Gongsun Qingke (公孙庆克). However, during the reign of Emperor An of Han (106-125), Qing Feng's descendants were forced to change their surname as it broke the naming taboo of Emperor An's father, Liu Qing (刘庆). Thus, they changed their surname from Qing (庆) to He (贺), both meaning "to celebrate".

From the name of the ancient state of Jia, located in present-day Shanxi province. During his reign (1020 BC - 996 BC), King Kang of Zhou granted the state of Jia to his cousin Gongming (公明), who would later be known as Jia Bo (贾伯). The state of Jia was later conquered by the state of Jin during the Spring and Autumn period (771 - 476 BC), and Jia Bo’s descendants adopted Jia as their surname.

From the State of Lai in the early Zhou Dynasty (1046 BC). Duke Shu Ying was conferred the title of "Duke of Lai", ruling over a territory in modern-day Henan province. This was his reward for assisting his elder brother, King Wu of Zhou (the first King of Zhou Dynasty, reign 1046–1043 BC) in defeating the Shang dynasty. His descendants subsequently adopted the name of the state as their surname. 

When the state of Lai was conquered by the Kingdom of Chu in 538 BC, the Lais dispersed to the south; many even changed their surname to escape persecution. Some fled to the neighboring states of Luo 羅 and Fu 傅, adopting these states' names as their new surnames. For this reason, the Lai, Luo, and Fu clans are believed to share some common ancestry.

From the name of the city of Zhao, in present-day Shanxi province. 

Mu Wang, king of the Zhou dynasty (1001–947 BC), was noted for his campaigns and journeys to distant lands and for his expansion of the Chinese empire. According to legend, he once traveled to the Kunlun mountains, then west of China, to see the Queen Mother of the West. After arriving, he learned of military attacks at home, so his chariot driver, Zao Fu, obtained eight marvelous steeds which took them back at a rate of a thousand li (500 miles) a day, so that they were able to defend the capital. In recognition of his service, Mu Wang granted to the charioteer Zao Fu the city of Zhao, and his descendants subsequently adopted Zhao as their surname.

The surname reached new heights of prominence during the Song dynasty (960 - 1279 AD), as it was the surname of the Song imperial family.

From the name of a state that existed during the Xia (2205–1766 BC) and Shang (1766–1122 BC) dynasties. At a much later date, descendants of the state’s rulers adopted the state name Deng as their surname. 

During the Five Dynasties (10th cent AD), the king of Nan Tang named his 8th son Li Cong Yi, the duke of Deng. After Nan Tang was eliminated, the people of the Deng kingdom became fugitives and used Deng as their last name (instead of Li) to avoid persecution.

The surname Qiu can trace its roots back to Jiang Ziya (姜子牙), a military advisor at the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 - 256 BC) who would later found the powerful state of Qi. The capital of Qi was a place named Yingqiu (营丘), located in present-day Shandong province. Some of Jiang Ziya’s descendants thus adopted Qiu (丘) as their surname. Thousands of years later, in 1725 AD, the Yongzheng Emperor of the Qing Dynasty decreed that a naming taboo was placed on the name of Confucius, which was Kong Qiu (孔丘). As a result, many people with the surname Qiu (丘) added a part meaning “place” (阝) to their surname, forming the word “邱” (which is still pronounced Qiu).

From the name of the ancient state of Shao (召 or 邵), located in present-day Shaanxi province. At the start of the Zhou Dynasty (1046-256 BC), a high-ranking minister named Shao Gong Shi (召公奭), or Shao Kang Gong (召康公), was granted the state of Shao. Some of his descendants would eventually adopt Shao (邵) as their surname.

The surname Zou has two different origins. The first originates from Zheng Kao Fu (正考父), a nobleman from the state of Song during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). He was granted the region of Zou (located in present-day Shandong province), and his descendants adopted Zou as their surname. The second origin can trace its roots to the ancient state of Zhulou (邾娄), whose name would later be changed to Zou during the Warring States period (475-221 BC). After the state of Zou was conquered by the state of Chu, its descendants adopted Zou as their surname too.

The Zheng surname originated from an ancient state located in present-day Henan Province. Descendants of King Wu Ding of the Shang dynasty (1250-1192 BC) adopted the name Zheng in memory of their ancestral state after being displaced during the Zhou conquest of 1046 BC. The name carries meanings of establishment and nation, reflecting the clan's royal heritage and territorial significance throughout subsequent periods of Chinese history.

The surname Hao can trace its roots back to the Shang dynasty, when King Yi (乙) granted his son Qi (期) the region of Haoxiang (郝乡), located in present-day Shaanxi province. His descendants would adopt Hao as their surname.

From an ancient kingdom located in modern-day Shanxi province. The Guos are believed to be descendants of the Zhou kings. 

A younger brother of the famed virtuous Duke Wen Wang (12th cent BC) was granted the kingdom of "Guo" and given the name "Prince Guo Shu". The original character for Guo kingdom, 虢, means "to hunt and flay a tiger", indicating that Prince Guo Shu was a brave warrior. In 658 BC, the state of Guo was annexed by the State of Jin, and descendants of the prince scattered. Eventually, they adopted a different character for their surname Guo.

Today, Guo is a multi-ethnic surname, which has been adopted by Muslim Hui, Mongolian, Manchu, and other ethnic groups throughout the centuries.

The surname Jin can trace its roots back to Shaohao (少昊), said to be the Yellow Emperor’s son. He was also known by the name Jintian (金天氏). After he died, some of his descendants adopted Jin as their surname. Another known origin of the surname Jin is from Jin Midi (金日䃅), a Xiongnu prince who pledged loyalty to the Han Dynasty. Impressed with his capabilities, Emperor Wu of Han (157-87 BC) granted him the surname Jin, which his descendants still bear till this day.

The Zhong family traces its ancestry to Tang of Shang, the first king of the Shang dynasty. A key figure in establishing the surname was Zhong Jie, who fled to Zhangge in Henan after his father, Zhongli Mei, a general under Xiang Yu, was defeated; Zhong Jie is considered the forefather of the Zhong family. The clan remained prominent through military leadership and political service across successive Chinese dynasties, later spreading throughout southern China and overseas.

The surname Qian can ultimately trace its roots back to Peng Zu (彭祖), a descendant of Emperor Zhuanxu who is said to have lived up to 800 years old. Peng Zu’s descendant, Peng Fu (彭孚), worked as a treasurer (钱府上士) during the reign of King Wen of Zhou (1125-1051 BC). His descendants would adopt Qian (钱) as their surname, which means “money” in Chinese.

The surname Yan has a few different origins. During his reign, King Wu of Zhou granted Zhong Yi (仲弈) the region of Yan. Later, King Zhao of Zhou and Duke Cheng of Jin would each grant one of their sons a region also known as Yan. It is said that the descendants from these three regions would all adopt Yan as their surnames.

The surname Lu has two origins, the first of which can trace its roots back to Lu Zhong (陆终), a great-grandson of Emperor Zhuanxu. Lu Zhong was granted the region of Luxiang (陆乡) in present-day Shandong province, and his descendants adopted Lu as their surname. The second origin story states that Duke Xuan of Qi (350-301 BC) granted the same region of Luxiang to his youngest son, Prince Tong (公子通), or Tian Tong (田通). His descendants also came to adopt Lu as their surname.

Descendants of legendary Emperor Shun, the Chen surname originated when Zhou King Wu Wang granted the region of Chen to Gui Man, a descendant of Emperor Shun, around 1046 BC after overthrowing the Shang dynasty. His descendants adopted the surname Chen, later honouring him posthumously as their founding ancestor, Chen Hugong. The name means "old" or "antiquated." Today Chen is the most prevalent surname in southern China and among the Chinese diaspora, with an estimated 70 million bearers worldwide, especially common in Fujian and Guangdong provinces.

From the name of a state called Han, which existed during the early part of the Western Zhou dynasty (1122–771 BC), in present-day Shaanxi province. This was the fief of a younger brother of Cheng Wang, second king of the Zhou dynasty. The state of Han was later annexed by the state of Jin, but the area was enfeoffed by the Jin ruler to Wu Zi, a descendant of Wen Wang. Wu Zi’s descendants eventually adopted the name of the fief as their surname.

The surname Gu has two origins. The first origin is from the ancient state of Gu, located in present-day Henan province, which was founded during the Xia Dynasty. When it was conquered by King Tang of Shang, its descendants adopted Gu as their surname. The second origin can trace its roots back to Goujian (勾践), King of Yue, who reigned in the late Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC). During the Han Dynasty (202 BC - 220 AD), a descendant of Goujian was granted the city of Kuaiji in present-day Zhejiang province, and known as Lord Guyu (顾余侯). His descendants would eventually adopt Gu as their surname as well.

From an honorific title borne by a prince of the state of Zhao during the Warring States period (403–221 BC). He was awarded the title Noble Ma Fu (literally "Tamer of Horses") after repeatedly distinguishing himself in battle as a general in charge of the cavalry. Subsequently, his descendants adopted part of the honorific title, Ma, as their surname. The Mas' ancestral home is in modern-day Shaanxi province.

Today, Ma is frequently adopted by Chinese Muslim and Turkic ethnic groups, as a translation of the surname 'Muhammad', and as a reminder of their nomadic culture and ancestry.

From the name of an area called Gao, in the ancient state of Qi (modern-day Shandong province) during the Western Zhou dynasty (1122–771 bc). The Gaos trace their ancestry to the Grand Duke of Qi's whose son was granted the land of Gao. Subsequently, his descendants adopted Gao as their surname, in his honor.

From the name of the ancient state of Wei, located in present-day Shanxi province. During the Spring and Autumn period (771 - 476 BC), Duke Xian of Jin granted the newly-conquered region of Wei to Jin nobleman Bi Wan (毕万). Later in 403 BC, the state of Jin was partitioned between rival families into the three states of Han, Zhao, and Wei, of which the state of Wei was ruled by Bi Wan’s descendants. Bi Wan’s descendants would later adopt Wei as their surname.

The Huang surname derives from the character meaning "yellow" and traces back to the legendary Yellow Emperor, Huang Di (2697-2595 BC). Most Huang descendants trace their ancestry to one of three kingdoms established during the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, with links also drawn to the Dong Yi tribe's "Huang Yi" group. During the Jin dynasty, northern invasions drove the clan southward into Fujian, with later migrations to Guangdong during the Tang dynasty, from where the surname eventually spread throughout Southeast Asia.

The surname Li originates from the ancient state of Li, located in present-day Shanxi province. The state of Li already existed during the Shang Dynasty, but was later conquered by King Wen of Zhou. King Wen then granted the state of Li to a descendant of Emperor Yao. Eventually, during during the Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BC), the state of Li was conquered by the state of Jin. Both the descendants from the earlier and later state of Li would adopt Li as their surname.

The surname Long has multiple origins. One of the origins traces its roots back to Emperor Yao. Emperor Yao’s descendant, Liu Lei (刘累), was the Keeper of Dragons for King Kong Jia during the Xia Dynasty. Some of Liu Lei’s descendants would eventually adopt Long (龙) as their surname, which means “dragon” in Chinese. Another origin states that Emperor Shun had an official named Long, and his descendants would adopt Long as their surname as well.

The surname Gong has multiple origins. One of them traces its roots back to Gonggong (共工), a descendant of the Yan Emperor who was in charge of waterworks, and later deified as the Water God. In turn, Gonggong's descendants adopted Gong (共) as their surname. Later, some branches added the word for dragon (龙) to their surname to form a new surname, Gong (龚). Another origin states that the surname is ultimately derived from the ancient state of Gong (共国) in present-day Henan province. Some of its descendants would also adopt Gong (共) as their surname, and later add the word for dragon (龙) to form Gong (龚) as well.
